Elko|United States of America.f: The first commercial airmail flight in the US landed at Elko in 1926, flying in from Pasco, Washington.

Abilene|United States of America.f: This Texas city took its name from Abilene, Kansas, the original endpoint of the Chisholm Trail.

Cortez|United States of America.f: A Republic of China Air Force U-2 spy plane glided to a night emergency landing at Cortez in 1959 after its engine flamed out.

Sault Ste. Marie|United States of Americ.f: Settled by French colonists in 1668, it is the oldest city in Michigan.

Show Low|United States of America.f: The town got its name from a poker game in which Corydon Cooley won a 100,000-acre ranch by showing low, the deuce of clubs.

Clovis|United States of America.f: A distinctive stone spear point found near Clovis in 1929 gave its name to the Clovis culture of early Americans.

Sitka|United States of America.f: Sitka's O'Connell Bridge, completed in 1972, was the first vehicular cable-stayed bridge in the United States.

Punta Gorda|United States of America.f: In 1896 a Florida newspaper called Punta Gorda the world's greatest phosphate shipping point.

Monterey|United States of America.f: In 1995 California's governor proclaimed Monterey the Language Capital of the World.

Greenville (NC)|United States of America.f: Founded as Martinsborough in 1771, the town was renamed Greenesville in 1786 for Revolutionary War general Nathanael Greene.

Tupelo|United States of America.f: On February 7, 1934, Tupelo became the first city to receive power from the Tennessee Valley Authority.

Branson|United States of America.f: Harold Bell Wright's 1907 novel The Shepherd of the Hills became a best seller and made Branson a tourist destination.

McAllen|United States of America.f: McAllen's foreign-trade zone, commissioned in 1973, was the first inland foreign-trade zone in the United States.

Telluride|United States of America.f: Butch Cassidy robbed the San Miguel Valley Bank in Telluride in June 1889 and got away with about $24,580.

Waco|United States of America.f: In 1930 Waco outfielder Gene Rye hit three home runs in a single inning, the only professional player ever to do so.

Liberal|United States of America.f: Liberal reportedly got its name because travelers said "That's very liberal of you" to a settler who gave out free water.

Brainerd|United States of America.f: In 1933 Baby Face Nelson and his gang held up the First National Bank of Brainerd.

Lynchburg|United States of America.f: James Albert Bonsack of Lynchburg invented the first cigarette-rolling machine in 1880.

Jacksonville (NC)|United States of Ameri.f: In 2016 Jacksonville became the first jurisdiction to adopt a paid holiday honoring the 13th Amendment.

Pullman|United States of America.f: Once called Three Forks, the town was renamed Pullman in 1881 after the railroad sleeping-car magnate George Pullman.

Quincy|United States of America.f: About 12,000 people watched the 1858 Lincoln-Douglas debate in Quincy, the largest crowd of any debate in the series.

Kearney|United States of America.f: The extra e in Kearney was reportedly added by postmen who kept misspelling the town's name until the spelling stuck.

Redmond|United States of America.f: The Forest Service has based all of Oregon's firejumpers at Redmond's Roberts Field since 1981.

Huntington|United States of America.f: Huntington was founded in 1871 as the western end of the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway and named for its founder, Collis P. Huntington.

Traverse City|United States of America.f: The bay it sits on was named by French voyageurs who made la grande traverse, the long crossing, over its mouth.

Islip|United States of America.f: Islip recorded 13.57 inches of rain in 24 hours on August 12 and 13, 2014, a New York state record.

Johnstown|United States of America.f: Johnstown is home to the Inclined Plane, billed as the world's steepest vehicular inclined plane.

Lexington|United States of America.f: In 1958 Lexington enacted the nation's first urban growth boundary to protect the horse farms around it.

Lewisburg|United States of America.f: Lewisburg's Carnegie Hall, built in 1902, is one of only four Carnegie Halls still in continuous use in the world.

Redding|United States of America.f: Redding began as Poverty Flats until the Central Pacific Railroad bought land there in 1868 for a northern terminus.

Grand Island|United States of America.f: Grand Island is named for La Grande Isle, an island formed by the Wood and Platte rivers that French traders knew.

Watertown (NY)|United States of America.f: Watertown's Paddock Arcade, built in 1850, is the oldest continuously operating enclosed mall in the United States.

Worcester|United States of America.f: Candlepin bowling was invented in Worcester by Justin White in 1879.

Truckee|United States of America.f: Truckee received 444.3 inches of snow in the 1951 to 1952 season.

College Station|United States of America.f: The city owes its name and existence to Texas A&M, which opened in 1871 along a railroad.

Wenatchee|United States of America.f: In 1931 Clyde Pangborn and Hugh Herndon landed near Wenatchee, completing the first nonstop flight across the Pacific.

Hagerstown|United States of America.f: Hagerstown is nicknamed the Hub City for the many railroads and roads that converged on it.

Mammoth Lakes|United States of America.f: A 1971 lawsuit by Mammoth Lakes residents extended California's environmental review law to private developments.

Vernal|United States of America.f: Vernal's Bank of Vernal was built with some 80,000 bricks mailed by parcel post from Salt Lake City, 180 miles away.

Columbus (GA)|United States of America.f: Columbus has the longest urban whitewater rafting and kayaking course in the world, at 2.5 miles.
